elements.id-string-410: Concisely, we investigate ``anti-rotors" -  novel structures underlying an algebra that are associated with a trove of computable algebra isomorphism invariants.
elements.id-string-411: Given a real unital associative algebra $A$ of nonzero finite dimension $n$ where the vector space of elements $\mathbb{R}^n$ is assumed to have the standard topology, an \mbox{anti-rotor} is the additive group of symmetric linear transformations that annihilate the infinitesimal rotation tensor associated with a chosen nonlinear unary operation implied by the axioms of an algebra.
elements.id-string-412: Since we are dealing with Euclidean $\mathbb{R}^n$, for computational purposes we can employ the standard basis in the context of the usual dot product `` $\cdot$ ", and for $s\in A$ we write $s=(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ with that understanding.
elements.id-string-413: For reasons indicated below, we will also write a differential 1-form as a formal dot product of an ordered $n$-tuple of vector field components and the ordered $n$-tuple $\mathfrak{d}s \equiv (dx_1,\dots, dx_n)$.
elements.id-string-414: Thus, for choice of the multiplicative inversion operation as defined by $s\mapsto s^{-1}$ in a suitable neighborhood of the algebra's multiplicative identity $\mathbf{1}_A$, the 1-form dual to the implied vector field is written as the formal expression $s^{-1}\cdot \mathfrak{d}s$ as referenced to the standard basis.
elements.id-string-415: The infinitesimal rotation matrix is then expressed by $d(s^{-1}\cdot \mathfrak{d}s)$, and the rotor (also known as the curl) is its Hodge dual.
elements.id-string-416: The anti-rotor specific to this choice of unary operation (i.e., $s\mapsto s^{-1}$ as above) is then,
elements.id-string-417: \begin{equation} \mathfrak{u}_A \equiv \{L\in M_n(\mathbb{R}): L^T=L \text{ and } d(\left[L(s^{-1})\right]\cdot \mathfrak{d}s)  = 0\},\end{equation} where superscript $^T$ indicates transpose or dual vector as applicable.  The \mbox{1-form} $\left[L(s^{-1})\right]\cdot \mathfrak{d}s$ can be alternatively written as another formal expression, $(s^{-1})^TL\mathfrak{d}s$, with both $s$ and $\mathfrak{d}s$ understood to be column arrays. We have introduced the \mbox{$n$-tuple} of differentials $\mathfrak{d}s$ because both $\left[L(s^{-1})\right]\cdot \mathfrak{d}s$ and $(s^{-1})^TL\mathfrak{d}s$ are convenient formats that streamline \mbox{various proofs}.  When dealing exclusively with unital algebras, there are reasons to suspect that the multiplicative inversion operation sufficiently represents the above set of an algebra's implied nonlinear unary operations vis-a-vis invariants derivable from anti-rotors, though presently this is formulated as a conjecture.  If the conjecture is false, the purview of the analysis expands accordingly.  In general, we take ``anti-rotor" to be defined by (\ref{8/30/24.3}), except when we consider homological issues, where nonunital algebras (in particular, proper ideals) are unavoidable.  In the latter setting, we can replace $s^{-1}$ in (\ref{8/30/24.3}) with $s^2$.  But unless stated otherwise (such as in the above instance), use of the term ``algebra" in the following means a member of the class of algebras described at the beginning of the second sentence in the first paragraph of this subsection. Nevertheless, some generalization of our results is possible (although we deal with nonunital algebras and some not associative algebras, in this paper we do not examine the possibility of extending the approach to complex algebras or infinite-dimensional algebras).  As we have noted, an anti-rotor is an abelian group under matrix addition.  More specifically, it is a real vector space having (it turns out) nonzero finite dimension.  However, that description does not adequately capture the structure of this entity, because the matrix product is intrinsic to the important mapping of an anti-rotor to a group of path-independent integrals, $\mathfrak{u}_A \mapsto \int_{{\bf 1}_A}^s [\mathfrak{u}_At^{-1}]\cdot \mathfrak{d}t$ (where the notation $\mathfrak{u}_A t^{-1}$ means $\{L(t^{-1}): L\in \mathfrak{u}_A\}$, and $\int_{{\bf 1}_A}^s [\mathfrak{u}_At^{-1}]\cdot \mathfrak{d}t$ means $\{\int_{{\bf 1}_A}^s [L(t^{-1})]\cdot \mathfrak{d}t: L\in \mathfrak{u}_A \}$).  The matrix product is also an intrinsic part of a functor mapping the category of $A$-bimodules to a category of anti-rotors.  Accordingly, anti-rotors are better thought of as objects in a particular category comprised of symmetric matrices with entries that are linear combinations of the components of a $k$-tuple of real parameters, where the morphisms are defined utilizing the matrix product.  This reflects the easily demonstrated feature that $\mathfrak{u}_A$ can alternatively be cast as a symmetric \mbox{$(n\times n)$-matrix} $M_{\mathfrak{u}_A}$ whose entries are linear combinations of the components of an $m$-tuple of real parameters, $(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_m)$, where $m$ is the dimension of $\mathfrak{u}_A$ as a vector space - so that the members of $\mathfrak{u}_A$ are given by $M_{\mathfrak{u}_A}$ when its $m$ parameters are replaced by any set of $m$ real values.   The determinant of $M_{\mathfrak{u}_A}$, written as $\text{det}(M_{\mathfrak{u}_A})$, is a polynomial involving some or all of the $m$ parameters.  The foundation of our program now consists of two results easy enough to be almost called observations. The surprise is that these lead to recognition of \mbox{subtle structural} features that isomorphic algebras must share, and consequential combinatorial questions.  Such issues, including some future prospects, include the following.  \begin{enumerate} {\it The first foundational} result concerns the elegant manner in which \mbox{anti-rotors} transform.   For example, if $K:A_1\rightarrow A_2$ is an algebra isomorphism, then \begin{equation} \mathfrak{u}_{A_1} = K^T \mathfrak{u}_{A_2} K, \end{equation} where $ K^T \mathfrak{u}_{A_2} K \equiv \{K^T L K:L\in\mathfrak{u}_{A_2}\}$. Among other things, this allows us to immediately extract various algebra isomorphism invariants from the anti-rotor.    Examples of such invariants include: \begin{enumerate}  The dimension $m$ of $\mathfrak{u}_A$.    The largest rank  of a member of $\mathfrak{u}_A$.   The smallest rank of a nonzero member of $\mathfrak{u}_A$.  The number of parameters on which $\text{det}(M_{\mathfrak{u}_A})$ actually depends.  Invariants of the real algebraic set, \begin{equation}V_\mathbb{R}({\rm det}(M_{\mathfrak{u}_A})) = \{(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_m)\in\mathbb{R}^m: {\rm det}(M_{\mathfrak{u}_A}) = 0 \}.\end{equation} \end{enumerate}  These represent a first family of invariants derived from the anti-rotor. {\it The second foundational result} (a consequence of (\ref{9/6/24.1})) leads to a complementary set of algebra isomorphism invariants.  Again let $K:A_1\rightarrow A_2$ be an algebra isomorphism, where for $s_1\in A_1$ we define $s_2\equiv Ks_1$.  Then for $s_1$ in an open ball centered at $\mathbf{1}_{A_1}$ consisting only of units, we have \mbox{the gratifying}, \begin{equation} \int_{{\bf 1}_{A_1}}^{s_1} \left[\mathfrak{u}_{A_1}t_1^{-1}\right]\cdot \mathfrak{d}t_1 = \int_{{\bf 1}_{A_2}}^{s_2} \left[\mathfrak{u}_{A_2}t_2^{-1}\right]\cdot \mathfrak{d}t_2, \end{equation} where an expression like $\int_{{\bf 1}}^{s} \left[\mathfrak{u}_At^{-1}\right]\cdot \mathfrak{d}t$ can be equivalently represented by the replacement of $\mathfrak{u}_A$ with $M_{\mathfrak{u}_A}$ to yield a parametrized integral that is interpreted as the collection of path-independent integrals resulting from all realizations of the $m$-tuple of parameters.  There are now invariants arising from enumeration of the results of integration of the above rational function integrands, i.e., concerning particular sums of rational functions, logarithms, and arctangents.  These constitute a second family of invariants (the three isomorphism classes of two-dimensional algebras each distinctly embody in pure elemental form the three invariants stemming from the above integrals).

An algebra will typically be denoted by $A$, sometimes subscripted, etc. The multiplicative identity of algebra $A$ is denoted as $\mathbf{1}_A$ or just $\mathbf{1}$ if no confusion arises.   As a vector, an element $s\in A$ has its dual vector denoted by $s^T$. The transpose of a linear operator $L$ is denoted by $L^T$. The implied nonlinear unary operations mapping into the algebra are each given by some linear combination of integer powers of an element, the inverse of some linear combination of integer powers of the element, or the product of a collection of such entities.  Among these, the multiplicative inversion operation stands out as one that is assuredly invertible on the space of units for any algebra.   Thus, focusing on the multiplicative inversion operation seems like a good place to start.  In fact, limiting our attention to {\it only} the multiplicative inversion operation as a replacement for the full algebra binary product operation is not quite as reductive as might be at first imagined, since that restricted focus does not entirely eliminate the influence of arbitrary products of algebra elements.  For example, consider elements $a,b$ where $a$ is a unit.  Using only vector space operations and the multiplicative inversion operation, we can construct the element $(a^{-1}-\epsilon b)^{-1}$, where $\epsilon$ is an appropriate choice of real number.  Let us suppose we are working in a representation, so that $a,b$ are matrices.  Then for small $\epsilon$, use of the \mbox{Neumann} series expansion implies $(a^{-1}-\epsilon b)^{-1} = a+\epsilon(ab)a+c$, where the spectral norm of $c$ is $O(\epsilon^2)$.  Thus, the product $ab$ clearly influences $(a^{-1}-\epsilon b)^{-1}$, despite the fact that the latter is constructed from $a$ and $b$ with only vector space operations and the multiplicative inversion operation.  Of more immediate significance for our ``bilinear binary product to nonlinear unary operator replacement" program is the fact that the multiplicative inversion operation can be used to approximate the nonlinear operations defined by taking positive or negative integer powers of an element.  For example, in the context of a matrix representation it is seen that, for a unit $s$, the Neumann series expansion leads to \mbox{$(\mathbf{1}-\epsilon s^{- 1})^{-1} - \mathbf{1}- \epsilon s^{-1} = \epsilon^2 s^{-2} + c$} where the spectral norm of $c$ is $O(\epsilon^3)$, etc.  At least in this sense, it seems that the multiplicative inversion operation, combined only with the vector space operations, subsumes the other nonlinear unary operations implied by the algebra's product operation (we will expand on this in \mbox{Section 5.2}).    egin{definition} With respect to elements $s$ of a given $n$-dimensional algebra $A$ written in the standard basis as $s= \left( egin{array}{ccc} x_1 \vdots x_n \end{array}ight)$, where these elements are in an open ball in $\mathbb{R}^n$ consisting only of units and whose central point is the multiplicative identity element $\mathbf{1}_A$, an {\it uncurling metric $L$} is a symmetric member of $M_n(\mathbb{R})$  satisfying,  egin{equation} d([Ls^{-1}]\cdot \mathfrak{d}s) = d\left((s^{-1})^T L \mathfrak{d}sight) = 0, \end{equation} where $\mathfrak{d}s \equiv \left( egin{array}{ccc} dx_1 \vdots dx_n \end{array}ight)$.  The real vector space of uncurling metrics is the algebra's {\it uncurling space}, $\mathfrak{u}_A$, also known as the {\it group of uncurling metrics}, also known as the {\it anti-rotor}. Thus,  (ef{4/7/23.1}) states that the curl of $Ls^{-1}$ vanishes (\mbox{$L$ ``uncurls" $s^{-1}$}). Given its additional layer of structure, an uncurling space is considerably more than a vector space.  Not surprisingly, an uncurling space is often more appropriately viewed as an object in a particular category where the morphisms make intrinsic use of the matrix product (as in Section 2.9 and Section 2.10). We can think of  ``anti-rotor" as emphasizing its meaning as an object subject to such a morphism, ``uncurling space" as recalling its status as a vector space (when its dimension is the important consideration), and ``group of uncurling metrics" as indicating the role of its members in facilitating integration (as in Section 2.6). The algorithm is contained in the proof of the following.   egin{proposition} The members of $\mathfrak{u}$ are the realizations of a symmetric $(n	imes n)$-matrix $M_{\mathfrak{u}}$ whose entries are linear combinations of the components of an $m$-tuple of real parameters, where $m$ is the dimension of $\mathfrak{u}$, and where each realization of $M_{\mathfrak{u}}$ as a real matrix results from replacing its $m$ parameters with the members of any set of $m$ members of $\mathbb{R}$. \end{proposition}   egin{proof} For an $n$-dimensional algebra with elements $s = (x_1,x_2,\dots,x_n)$ with respect to the standard basis, one initially takes $\mathfrak{u}$ to be a symmetric $(n	imes n)$-matrix $M$ whose upper triangular entries are each a different member of a set of $ rac{n(n+1)}{2}$ real parameters.  Computation of $s^{-1}$ produces a vector whose components are each a rational function of the $x_1,x_2,\dots,x_n$.  So far, $Ms^{-1}$ is a parametrized \mbox{$n$-dimensional} vector field whose components (which can easily be computed) are dependent on the initial set of parameters in $M$ and the $x_1,x_2,\dots,x_n$.  There are then $ rac{n(n-1)}{2}$ constraint equations that must be satisfied in order that (ef{4/7/23.1}) hold (for $L=M$).  Each of these equations has the form,  egin{equation}  rac{\partial}{\partial x_i}([Ms^{-1}]_j) -  rac{\partial}{\partial x_j}([Ms^{-1}]_i) = 0,\end{equation} where $[Ms^{-1}]_k$ indicates the $k$-th component of $Ms^{-1}$.  As noted, we can write $s^{-1} = (\hat{x}_1,\dots,\hat{x}_n)$, where each $\hat{x}_k$ is a rational function of the components of $s$.  Consequently, $[Ms^{-1}]_k$ is a linear combination of rational functions of the components $\hat{x}_1,\dots,\hat{x}_n$, where the coefficients defining this linear combination are linear combinations of various of the above parameters.  It follows that $ rac{\partial}{\partial x_p}([Ms^{-1}]_q)$ is again a sum rational functions of the components $x_1,\dots,x_n$, where this expression is again linear in the parameters.  Thus, multiplying both sides of (ef{9/2/24.2}) by a polynomial determined by the products of the polynomial denominators of the latter rational functions, the left-hand-side of (ef{9/2/24.2}) becomes a polynomial in the components of $s$, while remaining an expression that is linear in the parameters - and the right-hand-side of (ef{9/2/24.2}) remains zero. Hence, satisfaction of each of the $ rac{n(n-1)}{2}$ constraint equations (ef{9/2/24.2}) ultimately reduces to the requirement that a particular multivariate polynomial be {\it identically} zero.  After simplification of the polynomial to be a linear combination of independent monomials, each monomial term is then comprised of a coefficient consisting of a linear combination of some of the above $ rac{n(n+1)}{2}$ parameters, multiplying an expression consisting of a product of some of the components of $s$, each raised to some power.  Therefore, each of the above coefficients of these (independent) monomials are required to be zero.  Accordingly, the number of surviving independent parameters (i.e., parameters not required to be equated to some linear combination of other parameters, or set to 0) is in general reduced as the $ rac{n(n-1)}{2}$ constraint equations are successively treated.  $M$ is then modified as necessary, as each successive constraint equation is treated.  After treatment of all the constraint equations via the above steps defined by treatment of the constraint equations in some sequence, the final number $m$ of surviving independent parameters is the dimension of $\mathfrak{u}$, and the final entries of $M$ evidently yield the requisite $M_\mathfrak{u}$. \end{proof}  Consequently, $\mathfrak{u}$ can be represented as a symmetric $(n	imes n)$-matrix $M_{\mathfrak{u}}$ whose entries are particular linear combinations of $m$ independent parameters (where $m$ is the dimension of $\mathfrak{u}$), because each uncurling metric results from a single set of selected real values for those parameters. On the other hand (despite some concrete results listed in Section 1.1), it is likely that many of these Combinatorial problems will be very difficult.  Concerning the general question of the distribution of $n$-dimensional algebras into distinct ``bins" (i.e., classes) defined by the anti-rotor dimension, according to the proof of Proposition ef{9/2/24.1}, $\mathfrak{u}$ is derived from an initial set of $ rac{n(n+1)}{2}$ parameters, but these are then subjected to  $ rac{n(n-1)}{2}$ constraint equations.  One might then expect to be finally left with $ rac{n(n+1)}{2} -  rac{n(n-1)}{2} = n$ parameters - i.e., $	ext{dim}(\mathfrak{u}) = n$ (so there would only be a single nonempty bin).  Of course, this reasoning is faulty.  Consider the analogous problem of finding the symmetric matrices $L$ that satisfy (ef{4/7/23.1}) except that $s^{-1}$ is replaced with $s$ in that equation.  One quickly discovers that every constraint equation reduces to $0=0$, so that {\it every} symmetric $(n	imes n)$-matrix is a solution (the dimension of the solution space is $ rac{n(n+1)}{2}$).  So, if some of the constraint equations for uncurling metrics were subject to  that kind of thing, or if the $ rac{n(n-1)}{2}$ constraints did not constitute a set of $n$ independent constraints, perhaps $	ext{dim}(\mathfrak{u})$ could be some number greater than $n$.  Conversely, it might occur that a constraint equation eliminates more than one parameter, so that $	ext{dim}(\mathfrak{u})$ turns out to be less than $n$ (along these lines, see the proof of Theorem ef{4/8/22.1}).  On the other hand, we still might guess that $	ext{dim}(\mathfrak{u}) = n$ would define the most popular bin.  In fact, for all three isomorphism classes of two-dimensional algebras, Table I (Section 2.7) indicates that \mbox{$	ext{dim}(\mathfrak{u}) = 2$}.  For the three-dimensional algebras, Table II indicates that five of the six algebra isomorphism classes satisfy $	ext{dim}(\mathfrak{u}) = 3$, although the sixth satisfies $	ext{dim}(\mathfrak{u}) = 2$.  Moreover, as regards the four-dimensional algebras, it turns out that $	ext{dim}(\mathfrak{u}_{M_2(\mathbb{R})}) = 1$ (as follows from Theorem ef{4/8/22.1}). So a precise understanding of the distribution of $n$-dimensional algebras into the bins/classes defined by $	ext{dim}(\mathfrak{u})$ remains a goal.  However, Corollary ef{8/17/22.1} is a first general result relevant to a different aspect of the distribution of $n$-dimensional algebras into bins/classes defined by the anti-rotor dimension, as it indicates that if the anti-rotor is one-dimensional and has a nonsingular member then the algebra is simple. As we have noted, an anti-rotor is an abelian group under matrix addition.  More specifically, it is a real vector space having (it turns out) nonzero finite dimension.  However, that description does not adequately capture the structure of this entity, because the matrix product is intrinsic to the important mapping of an anti-rotor to a group of path-independent integrals, $\mathfrak{u}_A \mapsto \int_{{\bf 1}_A}^s [\mathfrak{u}_At^{-1}]\cdot \mathfrak{d}t$ (where the notation $\mathfrak{u}_A t^{-1}$ means $\{L(t^{-1}): L\in \mathfrak{u}_A\}$, and $\int_{{\bf 1}_A}^s [\mathfrak{u}_At^{-1}]\cdot \mathfrak{d}t$ means $\{\int_{{\bf 1}_A}^s [L(t^{-1})]\cdot \mathfrak{d}t: L\in \mathfrak{u}_A \}$).  Accordingly, anti-rotors are better thought of as objects in a particular category comprised of symmetric matrices with entries that are linear combinations of the components of a $k$-tuple of real parameters, where the morphisms are defined utilizing the matrix product.  This reflects the easily demonstrated feature that $\mathfrak{u}_A$ can alternatively be cast as a symmetric \mbox{$(n\times n)$-matrix} $M_{\mathfrak{u}_A}$ whose entries are linear combinations of the components of an $m$-tuple of real parameters, $(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_m)$, where $m$ is the dimension of $\mathfrak{u}_A$ as a vector space - so that the members of $\mathfrak{u}_A$ are given by $M_{\mathfrak{u}_A}$ when its $m$ parameters are replaced by any set of $m$ real values.   The determinant of $M_{\mathfrak{u}_A}$, written as $\text{det}(M_{\mathfrak{u}_A})$, is a polynomial involving some or all of the $m$ parameters.  The foundation of our program now consists of two results easy enough to be almost called observations. The surprise is that these lead to recognition of \mbox{subtle structural} features that isomorphic algebras must share, and consequential combinatorial questions.  Such issues, including some future prospects, include the following.  \begin{enumerate} {\it The first foundational} result concerns the elegant manner in which \mbox{anti-rotors} transform.   For example, if $K:A_1\rightarrow A_2$ is an algebra isomorphism, then \begin{equation} \mathfrak{u}_{A_1} = K^T \mathfrak{u}_{A_2} K, \end{equation} where $ K^T \mathfrak{u}_{A_2} K \equiv \{K^T L K:L\in\mathfrak{u}_{A_2}\}$. Among other things, this allows us to immediately extract various algebra isomorphism invariants from the anti-rotor. Thus, focusing on the multiplicative inversion operation seems like a good place to start.  In fact, limiting our attention to {\it only} the multiplicative inversion operation as a replacement for the full algebra binary product operation is not quite as reductive as might be at first imagined, since that restricted focus does not entirely eliminate the influence of arbitrary products of algebra elements.  For example, consider elements $a,b$ where $a$ is a unit.  Using only vector space operations and the multiplicative inversion operation, we can construct the element $(a^{-1}-\epsilon b)^{-1}$, where $\epsilon$ is an appropriate choice of real number.  Let us suppose we are working in a representation, so that $a,b$ are matrices. In this sense, the dual space is an elaboration of the usual algebra norm.   Furthermore, this elaboration is sometimes useful as regards an increased sensitivity to the components of an element. Concisely, we investigate ``anti-rotors" -  novel objects underlying an algebra that are associated with a trove of computable algebra isomorphism invariants. Given a real unital associative algebra $A$ of nonzero finite dimension $n$ where the vector space of elements $\mathbb{R}^n$ is assumed to have the standard topology, an \mbox{anti-rotor} is the additive group of symmetric linear transformations that annihilate the infinitesimal rotation tensor associated with a chosen nonlinear unary operation implied by the axioms of an algebra.  Since we are dealing with Euclidean $\mathbb{R}^n$, for computational purposes we can employ the standard basis in the context of the usual dot product `` $\cdot$ ", and for $s\in A$ we write $s=(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ with that understanding.  For reasons indicated below, we will also write a differential 1-form as a formal dot product of an ordered $n$-tuple of vector field components and the ordered $n$-tuple $\mathfrak{d}s \equiv (dx_1,\dots, dx_n)$. Thus, for choice of the multiplicative inversion operation as defined by $s\mapsto s^{-1}$ in a suitable neighborhood of the algebra's multiplicative identity $\mathbf{1}_A$, the 1-form dual to the implied vector field is written as the formal expression $s^{-1}\cdot \mathfrak{d}s$ as referenced to the standard basis.  The infinitesimal rotation tensor is then expressed by $d(s^{-1}\cdot \mathfrak{d}s)$, and the rotor (also known as the curl) is its Hodge dual. The anti-rotor specific to this choice of unary operation (i.e., $s\mapsto s^{-1}$ as above) is then, \begin{equation} \mathfrak{u}_A \equiv \{L\in M_n(\mathbb{R}): L^T=L \text{ and } d(\left[L(s^{-1})\right]\cdot \mathfrak{d}s)  = 0\},\end{equation} where superscript $^T$ indicates transpose or dual vector as applicable.  The \mbox{1-form} $\left[L(s^{-1})\right]\cdot \mathfrak{d}s$ can be alternatively written as another formal expression, $(s^{-1})^TL\mathfrak{d}s$, with both $s$ and $\mathfrak{d}s$ understood to be column arrays. We have introduced the \mbox{$n$-tuple} of differentials $\mathfrak{d}s$ because both $\left[L(s^{-1})\right]\cdot \mathfrak{d}s$ and $(s^{-1})^TL\mathfrak{d}s$ are convenient formats that streamline \mbox{various proofs}.  When dealing exclusively with finite dimensional unital algebras, there are reasons to suspect that the multiplicative inversion operation sufficiently represents the above set of an algebra's implied nonlinear unary operations vis-a-vis invariants derivable from anti-rotors, though presently this is formulated as a conjecture.  If the conjecture is false, the purview of the analysis expands accordingly.  On the other hand, nonunital algebras can be addressed by replacing $s^{-1}$ in (\ref{8/30/24.3}) with, say, $s^2$.  But unless stated otherwise, use of the term ``algebra" in the following means a member of the class of algebras described at the beginning of the second sentence in the first paragraph of this subsection, and (for reasons that will become clear) we take the anti-rotor to be defined by (\ref{8/30/24.3}).  Nevertheless, some generalization of our results is possible (we will have limited dealings with nonunital algebras and not associative algebras, but we do not examine the possibility of extending the approach to infinite-dimensional algebras or complex algebras).  As we have noted, an anti-rotor is an abelian group under matrix addition.  More specifically, it is a real vector space having (it turns out) nonzero finite dimension.  However, that description does not adequately capture the structure of this entity, because the matrix product is intrinsic to the important mapping of an anti-rotor to a group of path-independent integrals, $\mathfrak{u}_A \mapsto \int_{{\bf 1}_A}^s [\mathfrak{u}_At^{-1}]\cdot \mathfrak{d}t$ (where the notation $\mathfrak{u}_A t^{-1}$ means $\{L(t^{-1}): L\in \mathfrak{u}_A\}$, and $\int_{{\bf 1}_A}^s [\mathfrak{u}_At^{-1}]\cdot \mathfrak{d}t$ means $\{\int_{{\bf 1}_A}^s [L(t^{-1})]\cdot \mathfrak{d}t: L\in \mathfrak{u}_A \}$).  Accordingly, anti-rotors are better thought of as objects in a particular category comprised of symmetric matrices with entries that are linear combinations of the components of a $k$-tuple of real parameters, where the morphisms are defined utilizing the matrix product.  This reflects the easily demonstrated feature that $\mathfrak{u}_A$ can alternatively be cast as a symmetric \mbox{$(n\times n)$-matrix} $M_{\mathfrak{u}_A}$ whose entries are linear combinations of the components of an $m$-tuple of real parameters, $(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_m)$, where $m$ is the dimension of $\mathfrak{u}_A$ as a vector space - so that the members of $\mathfrak{u}_A$ are given by $M_{\mathfrak{u}_A}$ when its $m$ parameters are replaced by any set of $m$ real values.   The determinant of $M_{\mathfrak{u}_A}$, written as $\text{det}(M_{\mathfrak{u}_A})$, is a polynomial involving some or all of the $m$ parameters.  The foundation of our program now consists of two results easy enough to be almost called observations. The surprise is that these lead to recognition of subtle structural features that isomorphic algebras must share, and consequential combinatorial questions.  Such issues (which are new, so far as we know), including some future prospects, include the following.  \begin{enumerate} {\it The first foundational} result concerns the elegant manner in which \mbox{anti-rotors} transform.   For example, if $K:A_1\rightarrow A_2$ is an algebra isomorphism, then \begin{equation} \mathfrak{u}_{A_1} = K^T \mathfrak{u}_{A_2} K, \end{equation} where $ K^T \mathfrak{u}_{A_2} K \equiv \{K^T L K:L\in\mathfrak{u}_{A_2}\}$. Among other things, this allows us to immediately extract various algebra isomorphism invariants from the anti-rotor.    Examples of such invariants include: \begin{enumerate}  The dimension $m$ of $\mathfrak{u}_A$.    The largest rank  of a member of $\mathfrak{u}_A$. elements.id-string-911: The isomorphism invariants identified in the above corollary are clearly computationally straightforward.So, for example, an alternative system for algebra classification could be such that two algebras are in the same class if they have the same vector space dimension, they share the same values for the first three of the dimensional invariants of $\mathfrak{u}$ in the itemized list shortly following Theorem \ref{6/6/23.1}, and they have the same respective numbers of parameters multiplying bare rational function terms, logarithm terms, and arctangent terms, as identified in Corollary \ref{6/6/23.3}, i.e. arising from the mapping from $\mathfrak{u}$ to $ U$ defined by (\ref{11/7/20.2}).Of course, one can imagine augmenting the class definition by introducing additional computationally straightforward algebra invariants as may be identified.We will now illustrate this process using the real two-dimensional unital algebras - of which there are only three up to an isomorphism.

elements.id-string-913: Our program entails examination of the unary operations implied by the bilinear product operation of an algebra $A$ as a means of studying the algebra itself.

Each such operation, $f:D(A)ightarrow A$, is a vector field, where $D(A)$ is an appropriate domain in the algebra's vector space of elements.  In examination of a vector field it is of interest to consider the associated infinitesimal rotation tensor (the exterior derivative of the differential 1-form dual to the vector field; its Hodge dual is the curl of the vector field).  Its computation requires choice of a metric (i.e., a symmetric bilinear form, also referred to as a scalar product or metric tensor).  Specification of the standard topology as above entails imposition of the Euclidean inner product as the metric, allowing the computation to proceed.  However, this choice of metric is arbitrary, and can only be considered a default against which the results of all other choices should be compared.  Thus, with respect to a specific choice of unary operation $f$ to study, we are led to consideration of the mapping,  egin{equation} \slashed{	ext{S}}_f: \mathcal{M} ightarrow \delta	ext{Rot},\end{equation} with,  egin{equation} \slashed{	ext{S}}_f[\mu] = d\left([f(s)]^T \mu \mathfrak{d}sight).  \end{equation} In (ef{1/23/25.1}), $\mathcal{M}$ is the linear space of all possible metric tensors relevant to $\mathbb{R}^n$ (inclusive of metrics that are not necessarily positive definite and not necessarily nondegenerate), and $\delta	ext{Rot}$ is the linear space of possible infinitesimal rotation tensors relevant \mbox{to $\mathbb{R}^n$}.  Equation (ef{1/23/25.2}) is a formal expression interpreted with respect to the standard basis as follows.  Writing an algebra element as $s=(x_1,\dots,x_n)^T$, we define $\mathfrak{d}s \equiv (dx_1,\dots,dx_n)^T$. Thus, $\mu$ is a real symmetric matrix acted upon on the left by the row array $[f(s)]^T$ and on the right by column array $\mathfrak{d}s$.  On the right-hand-side of (ef{1/23/25.2}), $d(\cdot)$ represents the exterior derivative operation.  Hence, via the expected symbol manipulations, the right-hand-side of (ef{1/23/25.2}) yields the infinitesimal rotation tensor associated with the vector field $f$ with respect to the metric $\mu$ - or, equivalently, the infinitesimal rotation tensor of vector field $\mu f(s)$ with respect to the Euclidean metric.  $\slashed{	ext{S}}_f$ is a linear transformation taking symmetric tensors to skew-symmetric tensors. Consequently, we call $\slashed{	ext{S}}_f$ the ``Skewer" (the slash through ``symmetric" S represents a skewer, as with a shish-kabob). Since we assume the standard basis, $\mathcal{M}$ can be represented by a parametrized symmetric $(n	imes n)$-matrix with $ rac{n(n+1)}{2}$ independent parameters, i.e., it is given as a symmetric matrix with a different real parameter in each of its upper triangular entries.  Every possible metric tensor is given by some realization of the set of parameters (i.e., a realization results from any particular choice of $ rac{n(n+1)}{2}$ real values for the parameters).  Consequently, this parametrized symmetric matrix is mapped by the Skewer to a parametrized skew-symmetric matrix representing the resulting infinitesimal rotation tensors.  Each entry not on the main diagonal of the latter matrix is a rational function of the $n$ components of an element as a member of $\mathbb{R}^n$, and the above $ rac{n(n+1)}{2}$ parameters appear as coefficients of constituent rational function terms which sum to the entry.  While the image of the Skewer is thereby complicated, the kernel of the Skewer is another matter.  It is simply a subspace of $\mathcal{M}$;  the algebra's vector space of elements has vanished.  Thinking globally in the context of this less cluttered environment, we observe that {\it the selected operation $f$ produces a mapping from the set of algebras to the set of subspaces of $\mathcal{M}$ - whose analysis, for arbitrary $f$, might have much to say regarding algebra structure.} This paper is concerned with establishing the validity of that thesis. Since ``kernel of the Skewer" is a somewhat unwieldy term, we will henceforth instead refer to that entity as the ``anti-rotor" - because each of its members annihilates the infinitesimal rotation tensor.  Results in Section 4 and Section 8 justify beginning our analysis with the algebra's multiplicative inversion operation, i.e., the particular choice $f(s)=s^{-1}$.   egin{definition} With respect to elements $s$ of a given $n$-dimensional algebra $A$ written in the standard basis as $s= (x_1,\dots,x_n)^T$, where these elements are in an open ball in $\mathbb{R}^n$ consisting only of units and whose central point is the multiplicative identity element $\mathbf{1}_A$, an {\it uncurling metric $L$} is a symmetric member of the matrix algebra $M_n(\mathbb{R})$  satisfying,  egin{equation} d\left([Ls^{-1}]\cdot \mathfrak{d}sight) = d\left((s^{-1})^T L \mathfrak{d}sight) = 0, \end{equation} where $\mathfrak{d}s \equiv (dx_1,\dots,dx_n)^T$.  The real vector space of uncurling metrics is the algebra's {\it anti-rotor}, $\mathfrak{u}_A$.  It may also be denoted by $\mathfrak{u}$ if no confusion arises.    \end{definition}   A requisite open ball in the above definition always exists, as can be easily demonstrated by considering the left regular representation of the algebra.  The following simple result indicates the elegant manner in which anti-rotors transform.   egin{theorem}  If $K:A_1ightarrow A_2$ is an algebra isomorphism, then  egin{equation} \mathfrak{u}_{A_1} = K^T \mathfrak{u}_{A_2} K. \end{equation} \end{theorem}   egin{proof} By hypothesis, a nonsingular linear change of variable expression for the elements of $A_2$ in terms of the elements of $A_1$ can be written as $s_2= Ks_1$. \mbox{For $L_2\in \mathfrak{u}_{A_2}$} we obtain,  egin{equation} 0 = d\left((s_2^{-1})^T L_2 \mathfrak{d}s_2ight) =  d\left(((Ks_1)^{-1})^T L_2 \mathfrak{d}(Ks_1)ight) = d\left((s_1^{-1})^T  ig[K^T L_2K ig]\mathfrak{d}s_1ight),   \end{equation} where we have used Definition ef{7/21/23.1}, the commutativity of a differential with a linear transformation, and the isomorphism condition $(Ks_1)^{-1} = K(s_1^{-1})$.   It follows from (ef{9/21/23.1}) that every uncurling metric  of algebra $A_2$ is associated with an uncurling metric of $A_1$, i.e., from the last equality in (ef{9/21/23.1}) we have  $K^TL_2K\in\mathfrak{u}_{A_1}$.  An analogous argument employing $K^{-1}$ indicates that for $L_1\in\mathfrak{u}_{A_1}$ we have the associated $(K^{-1})^T L_1 K^{-1} \in \mathfrak{u}_{A_2}$.    Furthermore, $K^T L_2K\in\mathfrak{u}_{A_1}$ is such that $(K^{-1})^T [K^T L_2 K]K^{-1} = (K^T)^{-1} [K^T L_2 K]K^{-1} = L_2$.  Similarly, $(K^{-1})^T L_1K^{-1}\in\mathfrak{u}_{A_2}$ is such that $K^T[(K^{-1})^T L_1K^{-1}] K = L_1$.  The theorem follows from the implied bijection. \end{proof}  Computation of $\mathfrak{u}$ is straightforward in principle.  The algorithm is contained in the proof of the following. Computation of $s^{-1}$ produces a vector whose components are each a rational function of the $x_1,x_2,\dots,x_n$.  So far, $Ms^{-1}$ can be understood as a parametrized \mbox{$n$-dimensional} vector field whose components (which can easily be computed) are dependent on the initial set of parameters in $M$ and the $x_1,x_2,\dots,x_n$.  There are then $ rac{n(n-1)}{2}$ constraint equations that must be satisfied in order that (ef{4/7/23.1}) hold (for $L=M$).  Each of these equations has the form,  egin{equation}  rac{\partial}{\partial x_i}([Ms^{-1}]_j) -  rac{\partial}{\partial x_j}([Ms^{-1}]_i) = 0,\end{equation} where $[Ms^{-1}]_k$ indicates the $k$-th component of $Ms^{-1}$.  As noted, we can write $s^{-1} = (\hat{x}_1,\dots,\hat{x}_n)$, where each $\hat{x}_k$ is a rational function of the components of $s$.  Consequently, $[Ms^{-1}]_k$ is a linear combination of rational functions of the components $\hat{x}_1,\dots,\hat{x}_n$, where the coefficients defining this linear combination are linear combinations of various of the above parameters.  It follows that $ rac{\partial}{\partial x_p}([Ms^{-1}]_q)$ is again a sum rational functions of the components $x_1,\dots,x_n$, where this expression is again linear in the parameters.  Thus, multiplying both sides of (ef{9/2/24.2}) by a polynomial determined by the products of the polynomial denominators of the latter rational functions, the left-hand-side of (ef{9/2/24.2}) becomes a polynomial in the components of $s$, while remaining an expression that is linear in the parameters - and the right-hand-side of (ef{9/2/24.2}) remains zero. Hence, satisfaction of each of the $ rac{n(n-1)}{2}$ constraint equations (ef{9/2/24.2}) ultimately reduces to the requirement that a particular multivariate polynomial be {\it identically} zero.  After simplification of the polynomial to be a linear combination of independent monomials, each monomial term is then comprised of a coefficient consisting of a linear combination of some of the above $ rac{n(n+1)}{2}$ parameters, multiplying an expression consisting of a product of some of the components of $s$, each raised to some power.  Therefore, each of the above coefficients of these (independent) monomials are required to be zero. The determinant of $M_{\mathfrak{u}}$, written as ${m det}(M_{\mathfrak{u}})$, is a polynomial in some or all of the components of an ordered $m$-tuple of parameters, $(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_m)$.  If $m$ is small  we will denote the parameters using different Greek letters like $\alpha$, $ eta$, $\gamma$, etc.  With the above in mind, it is seen that (ef{5/23/23.1}) has immediate consequences - our first family of algebra isomorphism invariants resulting from the anti-rotor.   egin{corollary} The following are algebra isomorphism invariants.  egin{itemize}  The dimension $m$ of $\mathfrak{u}$. Invariants of the real algebraic set,  egin{equation}V_\mathbb{R}({m det}(M_{\mathfrak{u}})) = \{(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_m)\in\mathbb{R}^m: {m det}(M_{\mathfrak{u}}) = 0 \}.\end{equation} \end{itemize} \end{corollary}   \enlargethispage{1cm}  egin{definition} Let $L$ be an uncurling metric for some algebra $A$. The duality referred to in Definition ef{9/21/23.2} is easily appreciated.  Equation (ef{9/21/23.2}) can be rewritten as  \mbox{$\log\ell(s) =  rac{1}{\|\mathbf{1}\|^2}\int_{{ f 1}}^{s} \left[L t^{-1}ight]\cdot \mathfrak{d}t$.}   We can view this as a forward integral transform, mapping $L$ to $\log \ell(s)$.   The latter equation implies that an uncurling metric and its associated unital norm satisfy,   egin{equation} Ls^{-1}  = 
abla\left[\|{ f 1}\|^2\log  \ell(s)ight] =   \left( rac{\|{ f 1}\|^2}{ \ell(s)}ight)
abla \ell(s).\end{equation}  Due to invertibility of the multiplicative inversion operation,  (ef{11/7/20.1}) can be rewritten as  $Ls = \|\mathbf{1}\|^2 
abla\left[\log \ell(s^{-1})ight]$, where the right-hand-side is interpreted to mean the product of $\|\mathbf{1}\|^2$ with the gradient of $\log \ell$ which is then evaluated at $s^{-1}$.  The latter equation defines the inverse transform - where $L$ (which can be extracted from $Ls$) is obtained from $\log\ell(s)$ (this being an integral transform in the sense of distributions). In other words, groups of uncurling metrics and groups of unital norms are dual (where the duality between individual members of  $\mathfrak{u}_A$ and $\mathfrak{u}_A^d$ follows from an integral transform defined with respect to the multiplicative inversion operation $s\mapsto s^{-1}$).   Also note that according to (ef{11/7/20.1}), the pair $(L, \ell(s))$ characterizes the algebra's multiplicative inversion operation $s\mapsto s^{-1}$ in the portion of an open ball centered at $\mathbf{1}$ devoid of non-units that is orthogonal to the kernel of $L$.  If $L$ is nonsingular, this pair fully characterizes the inversion operation $s^{-1}$ in an open ball centered at $\mathbf{1}$ devoid of non-units.  For a given algebra, the set of all such pairs (where $L$ may or may not be singular) is an abelian group with respect to the binary operation defined by,  egin{equation}  ig(L_1, \ell_1(s) ig) ig(L_2, \ell_2(s) ig) \equiv  ig(L_1+L_2, \ell_1(s)  \ell_2(s) ig).\end{equation}
